pillar_reactions.evidence: Delivered from 00:41:31 and led with mobility, which is what he had asked for. He was already pre-sold — he had bought a kettlebell before the call on the strength of Trevor's videos, 'I've never worked out with a kettlebell. I went ahead and bought one, actually' — and he volunteered a positive reaction tied to his own life: 'that sounds very compelling. Yeah. I do travel a fair bit for work. And there you go. I guess there's always a gym that has a kettlebell.' He also endorsed the teach-a-man-to-fish framing unprompted: 'I like the fact that you guys teach a man to fish. Yeah, it's the right way to do it.' Enthusiasm sat alongside a lot of clarifying questions about his adjustable Bowflex bell and about whether posture gets corrected before loading.

Delivered at 00:45:46. He interrupted to check the mechanism against something he had already tried: 'Just a quick question there, 8 to 10 hour window would mean that you're, I don't know, and you're the expert here again, some sort of intermittent fasting, is that correct?... Effectively, I've done that in the past, I've skipped breakfast and I just have lunch and dinner, is that something along those lines?' He accepted the answer — 'That sounds fair, makes sense' — without enthusiasm. Notable that the rep's diagnosis was that he under-eats rather than over-eats, which the prospect did not push back on.

Delivered at 00:48:40 and correctly identified as the piece that matters for him, given two decades of starting and stopping. He accepted it at the time — 'Makes sense' — but returned to it repeatedly much later with the most detailed mechanical interrogation in the batch: Trevor's response time ('he's pretty responsive, I imagine' — answered as within 24 hours), how many hours a week he would actually get with Trevor, whether sessions are synchronous ('so I guess you're saying all of my sessions are basically me recording myself and sending him the video'), whether video feedback comes back as text or video, whether a live session is possible if he is struggling with form, and whether the app runs on Android. The answers were accurate but the reaction is clarifying-verging-on-deflating: he discovered the only live contact he gets is a single 30-minute onboarding call.

anchors.raw: It's not, not about the, um, I'm not thinking about the money. I'm just trying to think about. Because I know so little about the program, it's difficult for me to judge. Is it going to be enough?
anchors.note: The single most important signal on this call. The moment $9,000 and $6,000 were named he removed price from the conversation, and forty minutes later he reinforced it in the other direction: 'if that means that there's a higher dollar commitment to getting that comfort level, I'm even willing to work with that.' Nothing in his head competes with $6,000. The barrier was the six-month term and the absence of verification, and the rep nonetheless resolved it with a 80% discount on the first payment.

anchors.raw: I've never hired a personal trainer, but I've heard that typically the way it goes from my friends is they go to a gym, they hire a personal trainer, or they have someone come home and they work out with them, and typically there are references that are shared.
anchors.note: Not a price anchor but a service-norm anchor, and it is what generated the reference objection. His model of one-on-one coaching comes from friends who hire trainers in person and get referrals, and this offer matches neither half of that. He used it to argue that a higher-commitment purchase should carry more verification, not less.

anchors.raw: when I trained with P90X, I didn't talk to Tony Horton and he didn't give me any personal references, because it was like, okay, this is the video that you get, you work with that, that's it, right? This is not a training, not a one-on-one training, right? But over here, it's a one-on-one training commitment.
anchors.note: He is explicitly distinguishing rather than comparing — P90X is what he accepts without references because it is a video product, and he expects more from something sold as one-on-one. The uncomfortable implication, which he did not draw and the rep did not address, is that what he actually bought is much closer to the P90X model than to the personal-trainer model: a programme in an app, asynchronous video feedback, and one live call ever.

anchors.raw: I talked to my boss quite often about this stuff, and he's one of the fittest guys I personally know. And he works quite a bit as well... he keeps telling me, like, you know, you've got to figure out your why, if you don't know your why, it's never going to happen
anchors.note: A close, credible peer who is both very busy and very fit, and who has already sold him the premise that a strong why is the mechanism. The rep used this well, echoing it back at 00:48:40 — 'as your boss, we are all busy. But somehow, he's finding the discipline to do it.' It supports the purchase by normalising deliberate investment in health among people like him.

unmet_demand.want: Contactable customer references, ideally Bay Area clients with a similar lifestyle, willing to speak or email about their experience
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The company does not provide them. The rep stated it as policy — 'we cannot and we don't actually reveal customers' personal details apart from those who agreed that, yeah, I can take part and record an interview with Trevor' — leaving recorded testimonials on the website as the only verification available. The prospect's fallback was explicit: 'If that's not a possibility, I'll just go look at the testimonials and I'll make my mind up based on that.' This is the highest-value unmet demand in the batch: it consumed fifteen minutes, was never answered, and cost $4,800 of the sale.

unmet_demand.want: A physical assessment before being loaded, given self-suspected anterior pelvic tilt and a back that reliably fails under leg work
unmet_demand.why_unmet: No assessment of any kind exists. The rep confirmed it explicitly when asked: 'does he need me to be physically in a place where I can show him my workout setup?' — 'no, no, no'; 'Even like, what kind of shape I am in, does he need to look at that or no?' — 'No, no, no, no'; and 'it's your assessment that, that you say, like you've, you mentioned that you have back pain, right? So that's it.' The prospect asked the right question twice and was told the programme runs entirely on his own self-report.

unmet_demand.want: Live or synchronous coaching contact beyond the single onboarding call
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The model is asynchronous by design — 'you don't have to have a set meeting with him to go over the particular movement because it's asynchronous' — and the answer to a direct request for live form checking was that recorded video from different angles is sufficient. This is the third prospect in this batch to probe for live coaching cadence after Marian Samson and Sasa Svalina, and the second to be told plainly it does not exist.

Trevor has no slots before 10:15 Pacific and none at weekends in June or July. The prospect's entire plan for making this work is training in the morning before daycare drop-off, and the earliest onboarding he could take was a mid-workday slot nine days out. 'These are all times where I'm actually at work. So I'm just wondering, when does this day typically start, I guess? Is there anything between 6 and 8 a.m. that works for him, or no?' — 'I don't see that on his schedule, actually.'

unmet_demand.want: Evidence that clients starting from pain and poor posture, rather than from an already-fit baseline, have succeeded
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He named the gap in the testimonials precisely — 'I felt like those people were at least fitter than me to begin with when they started' — and the answer was an unevidenced assertion that such clients are the majority. No case study, no before-state example, no named client. The programme may well serve these people best; there is nothing on the shelf that shows it.
